config.title: Forms & Validation (TypeScript)

intro.title: Forms & Validation — Typed
intro.body: Forms are the primary way users interact with your application. TypeScript ensures your form data is predictable and validated at compile time, preventing runtime errors and improving developer experience.
intro.usecase: You're building a sign-up form for a new service. Users need to provide their name, email, and password with real-time validation feedback.

objectives: Create typed form state with useState
Handle input changes with TypeScript event types
Implement real-time validation with error state

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the react package.
steps.hint: You need two imports: React and useState from 'react'.
steps.whyThisMatters: React provides the foundation for building components, and useState lets us manage form state that changes over time.

thinkPrompt.question: What's the primary purpose of useState in a form component?
options: To handle form submission to a server
To manage and update form field values as the user types
thinkPrompt.correctAnswer: To manage and update form field values as the user types

steps.anchor: useState tracks form field values as they change, enabling reactive updates.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have access to React and useState.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've imported the essential React tools.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Check if you imported both React and useState.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember to import both React and useState from 'react'.

steps.title: Define the component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named SignUpForm that returns JSX.Element.
steps.hint: Use the function keyword or arrow function with proper TypeScript return type.
steps.whyThisMatters: Every React form needs a component container. TypeScript ensures our component has proper typing from the start.

thinkPrompt.question: What TypeScript type should a functional component return?

steps.anchor: Functional components in TypeScript typically return JSX.Element.
steps.expectedOutcome: A component skeleton ready for form logic.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! Your component is properly typed.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Make sure your component returns JSX.Element.
steps.feedbackWrong: Create a function component that returns JSX.Element.

steps.title: Define form state interface
steps.instruction: Inside the component (before any logic), define an interface for the form state with name, email, and password fields, all typed as strings.
steps.hint: Create an interface with three string properties.
steps.analogousExample: interface User { id: number; username: string; };
steps.whyThisMatters: TypeScript interfaces document the shape of your form data, making it clear what fields exist and their expected types.

thinkPrompt.question: Why define an interface for form state instead of using inline types?
options: Interfaces make the code run faster
Interfaces provide reusable, self-documenting type definitions
Multiple parts of your component — state, handlers, props — need to agree on the same shape. A named interface is the single source of truth; inline types force you to repeat or drift.
thinkPrompt.correctAnswer: Multiple parts of your component — state, handlers, props — need to agree on the same shape. A named interface is the single source of truth; inline types force you to repeat or drift.

steps.anchor: Correct: Without a named interface, you'd have to duplicate { email: string; password: string } in your useState, your submit handler, and anywhere else that touches that data. One rename breaks everything. The interface creates a single contract — change it once, TypeScript catches every mismatch automatically.
steps.simplerVersion: type FormData = { field1: string; field2: string; };
steps.expectedOutcome: A typed interface describing the form's data structure.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! Your interface clearly defines the form structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check that all three fields are present and typed as strings.
steps.feedbackWrong: Define an interface with name, email, and password as string properties.

steps.title: Initialize form state
steps.instruction: Use useState to create form state, typed with your interface, initialized with empty strings for all fields.
steps.hint: Call useState with an object containing empty string values.
steps.whyThisMatters: useState with proper typing ensures your form starts with valid initial values and prevents type errors during updates.

thinkPrompt.question: What should the initial form state typically be?
options: Empty strings or default values matching the interface
thinkPrompt.correctAnswer: Empty strings or default values matching the interface

steps.anchor: Form state should initialize with values that match the interface structure.
steps.expectedOutcome: Typed form state with empty initial values.
successCriteria: State is typed with the interface
Initial value has all three fields as empty strings
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! Your form state is properly typed and initialized.
steps.feedbackPartial: Make sure you're using your interface to type the state.
steps.feedbackWrong: Use useState with your interface type and initialize all fields as empty strings.

steps.title: Create the form JSX structure
steps.instruction: In the component's return statement, create a form element with three input fields for name, email, and password.
steps.whyThisMatters: The visual structure provides users with input fields to interact with. Semantic HTML improves accessibility.

thinkPrompt.question: Which HTML element should wrap related form inputs?

steps.anchor: The <form> element semantically groups inputs and handles submission events.
steps.expectedOutcome: Basic form structure with three input fields.
successCriteria: Inputs have appropriate types (text, email, password)
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! Your form structure is semantically correct.
steps.feedbackPartial: Make sure you're using <form> and three <input> elements.
steps.feedbackWrong: Return a <form> with three <input> elements for name, email, and password.

steps.title: Create change handler
steps.instruction: Create a handleChange function that updates the corresponding form field when any input changes.
steps.hint: The function should accept a ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> and update state using the input's name and value.
steps.whyThisMatters: Event handlers connect user input to state updates. TypeScript ensures we handle events with proper typing.

thinkPrompt.question: What TypeScript type should we use for input change events?

steps.anchor: ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> provides type-safe access to the input's value property.
successCriteria: Updates form state using e.target.name and e.target.value
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! Your handler is properly typed and functional.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check that your handler uses e.target.name to update the correct field.
steps.feedbackWrong: Create a function that accepts ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> and updates state based on e.target.name and e.target.value.

steps.title: Connect inputs to state and handler
steps.instruction: Wire each input to display the corresponding form state value and call your change handler on input events.
steps.hint: Add value and onChange attributes to each input.
steps.whyThisMatters: Two-way binding ensures the input displays current state and updates state on change, creating a controlled component.

thinkPrompt.question: What two attributes create a controlled input in React?

steps.anchor: value binds input to state, onChange updates state when user types.
steps.expectedOutcome: Inputs that display and update form state.
successCriteria: Inputs have value attributes bound to form state
Inputs have onChange attributes bound to handleChange
Each input has a name attribute matching its field
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! Your form is now fully controlled.
steps.feedbackPartial: Make sure each input has both value and onChange attributes.
steps.feedbackWrong: Add value={formState.field} and onChange={handleChange} to each input, with matching name attributes.

steps.title: Add real-time validation
steps.instruction: Add validation that displays an error message if the email doesn't contain '@' or if the password is less than 6 characters.
steps.hint: Create validation logic and conditionally render error messages near the inputs.
steps.whyThisMatters: Immediate feedback helps users correct errors before submission, improving user experience.

thinkPrompt.question: When should validation typically run in a form?

steps.anchor: Real-time validation provides immediate feedback, reducing user frustration.
steps.expectedOutcome: Conditional error messages based on input validity.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! Your form now provides helpful validation feedback.
steps.feedbackPartial: Make sure your validation runs on each change and messages appear conditionally.
steps.feedbackWrong: Add validation that shows errors when email lacks '@' or password is too short.
